Hennepin County by the numbers

Who bills and collects property tax in Hennepin County?

Two county offices split the work. The assessor sets market value and classification, and the treasurer's counter at the Government Center collects the money. Property tax questions go to the tax information line at 612-348-3011, staffed Monday through Friday until half past four, or to taxinfo@hennepin.us.

A Hennepin County parcel sits inside several taxing districts at once, usually the county, a city, a school district and some special districts. The county says more than 70 local governments levy on property here, and the auditor turns each levy and the assessment data into a rate for each district. If you plan to sell, the bill on your statement adds up every one of those pieces.

What does Hennepin County look like for someone selling a house?

Hennepin is the most populous county in Minnesota, with Minneapolis as its seat. The Territorial Legislature created it on March 6, 1852, and the mills at Saint Anthony Falls drove the early growth of the county. By 1970 the suburbs held more people than the cities for the first time, which is why a seller in Hopkins or Maple Grove deals with very different local rules than one in north Minneapolis.

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts page gives these numbers for the county:

  • 1,284,784 residents in the July 2025 estimate, on 554 square miles of land.
  • 539,493 households in 2020 to 2024, with 62.7% of homes owner occupied.
  • A median owner-occupied home value of $392,900 and median household income of $97,653.
  • 587,984 housing units and 3,491 building permits in 2025.

The county holds 22 school districts, including Minneapolis Public Schools, Edina, Minnetonka, Wayzata, Osseo Area and Anoka-Hennepin, and the district a house sits in is part of its tax bill.

When are Hennepin County property taxes due?

Half is due May 15 and half on October 15. When either date lands on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, the deadline slides to the next working day. Minnesota Statutes 279.01 states the same two installments as payable before May 16 and before October 16 when taxes on a parcel exceed $100.

Late payments carry a penalty. The statute sets 2 percent on homestead property and 4 percent on nonhomestead property the day after the due date, adds the same amount again on the first day of the next month, then 1 percent per month through December. Penalty stops growing at 8 percent for homestead and 12 percent for nonhomestead. Hennepin applies late payments to penalty first and taxes second.

One relief valve exists. An owner may ask the county to abate the penalty on a late payment once every ten years, for one half only, after the full tax is paid and with no older unpaid years on the parcel. The application for second half taxes is due November 30.

How do I pay Hennepin County property tax?

Online payment is open for real property. The county lists e-check, credit or debit card, PayPal and Venmo, and a payment counts as made the day it is submitted. Mobile home and personal property accounts have to use another method.

  • E-check costs nothing and is capped at $50,000 per transaction.
  • Cards, PayPal and Venmo are capped at $25,000 per transaction. Visa debit adds a $2.95 flat fee and other electronic methods add 2.29%, and the county keeps none of it.
  • In person, on the 6th floor of the Government Center at 300 South 6th Street, weekdays 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Card payments there carry a 2.49% service fee.
  • A drop box on the same floor takes checks payable to Hennepin County Treasurer, weekdays from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m.
  • By phone at 1-877-626-0017, or by mail to the Hennepin County Treasurer at A-600 Government Center, Minneapolis, MN 55487-0060, postmarked on or before the due date.

Direct payment withdraws from a bank account on May 15 and October 15. Forms must arrive by April 15 for the first half and September 15 for the second.

How is a Hennepin County value set and how do I appeal it?

The assessor assigns a market value as of January 2 each year and mails valuation notices in March. The county says it physically reviews every property once every five years. The value you see now drives the tax you pay the next year, so a notice that looks too high is worth reading closely.

Appeals start informally. Call the assessor whose number is printed on your notice, or go to an open book meeting if your city holds one. If that does not settle it, the formal route is a letter or appearance before the local board of appeal and equalization, then the county board in mid-June. To appear before the county board, call 612-348-7050 or email countyvalueappeal@hennepin.us by the date on the notice. The other formal path is Minnesota Tax Court, and under Minnesota Statutes 278.01 a district court petition for taxes payable in a given year must be filed by April 30 of that year.

Which Hennepin County cities run their own assessor?

Six cities handle assessment themselves, and an owner there calls the city instead of the county. Everywhere else the county assessor at 612-348-3046 answers the question.

  • Bloomington, 952-563-8722
  • Brooklyn Park, 763-493-8175
  • Eden Prairie, 952-949-8511
  • Minneapolis, 612-673-3000
  • Minnetonka, 952-939-8220
  • St. Louis Park, 952-924-2535

Calling the wrong office wastes the spring window, so check the notice mailed to the property before you dial.

What happens to unpaid property tax when I sell in Hennepin County?

Delinquent tax has to be cleared before the deed can be recorded. Minnesota Statutes 272.12 tells the auditor to check for delinquent taxes when a deed comes in for transfer, and the recorder will not accept the deed without the auditor's note that no delinquent taxes remain. The county's recording checklist repeats that properties with delinquent taxes may not be transferred.

Current-year tax is a separate matter. If you sell only part of a parcel, Statutes 272.121 asks for a treasurer's certification that the current year tax on the whole parcel is paid. On a normal whole-parcel sale, ask your title company how this year's tax gets split between you and the buyer, and get a payoff figure from the county if a half is still open.

Can a homeowner in Hennepin County reduce the tax bill?

Homestead status is the main lever. The county says you may qualify if you have a Social Security or individual taxpayer identification number, own the home in your own name rather than as a business entity, and live in it, or a relative does. A homesteaded property can qualify for a reduced classification rate, a reduced taxable market value and the state property tax refund.

Owners who just bought should check the taxpayer name and mailing address on the county property map and send a change form if either is wrong. The Property Watch email service tells an owner whenever a document is recorded against the parcel, which is useful when a payoff or release from an old loan is supposed to be recorded.

More questions about Hennepin County, MN Property Tax Guide

What are the Hennepin County property tax due dates?

May 15 for the first half and October 15 for the second half, with a Saturday, Sunday or holiday pushing the deadline to the next working day. A mailed check needs a postmark on or before the date.

Can I sell my Hennepin County house if the property taxes are unpaid?

Yes, as long as the delinquent amount is paid first. Minnesota Statutes 272.12 bars the deed from being recorded until the auditor confirms there are no delinquent taxes, so the payoff normally comes out of closing.

How do I contest my Hennepin County valuation?

Call the assessor listed on the March notice, then use the local board or the county board of appeal and equalization in spring. For the county board, phone 612-348-7050 or email countyvalueappeal@hennepin.us by the date on the notice.

Does Hennepin County charge a fee to pay by card?

Yes. Visa debit adds a $2.95 flat fee online and other electronic methods add 2.29%, all of which goes to the card processor. E-check online has no fee, and card payments at the counter carry 2.49%.

Who do I call with a Hennepin County property tax question?

Call property tax information at 612-348-3011 or email taxinfo@hennepin.us, Monday to Friday. For value questions, call the assessor at 612-348-3046 unless you live in a city that has its own assessor.

Dakota County by the numbers

Who do you call about property tax in Dakota County, Minnesota?

Two county groups split the work. Assessing Services sets value and classification (651-438-4200), and Property Taxation & Records bills, collects and handles delinquent years (651-438-4576). Walk-in service for both is at the Administration Center in Hastings, the county seat, at 1590 Highway 55.

Dakota County is the third most populous county in Minnesota, at about 457,710 people on the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate. The Minnesota and Mississippi Rivers form its northern and eastern edge, and Lakeville is its largest city.

What do sellers face in Dakota County's housing market?

Dakota County mixes dense suburbs in the north with farmland and small towns in the south. Burnsville, Eagan, Apple Valley, Lakeville, Rosemount and Hastings sit among the larger cities, while Farmington, Hampton, Randolph and Miesville keep an older street grid. Wikipedia reports that 54% of residents work outside the county, mostly in the Twin Cities core.

  • School districts include 196 (Rosemount-Apple Valley-Eagan), 191 (Burnsville-Eagan-Savage), 194 (Lakeville), 197 (West St. Paul-Mendota Heights-Eagan), 200 (Hastings) and Special School District 6 (South St. Paul).
  • Median value of owner-occupied homes is $381,000 for 2020 to 2024.
  • Median household income is $106,318, and median gross rent is $1,548.
  • Owner-occupied housing is 74.9% of the stock, and 185,931 housing units were counted in July 2025.

A higher home value usually means a bigger property tax bill, so a seller should read the statement before pricing. The county's Tax Estimator page lets you test a number.

When is property tax due in Dakota County?

Real property tax is due May 15 and October 15, and both 2026 dates have passed. Agricultural land and manufactured homes have a November 16 second-half date, which is tomorrow, since November 15 falls on a Sunday this year.

Dakota County property tax due dates by property type (Property Taxation and Records)
Property typeFirst halfSecond half
Real propertyMay 15Oct. 15
Manufactured homeAug. 31Nov. 16

Personal property on government-owned landMay 15Oct. 15

A payment mailed to the county must be postmarked on or before the due date or penalties apply. Under Minnesota Statutes section 279.01, homestead tax pays 2% after the due date and non-homestead 4%.

How can you pay Dakota County property tax?

The county lists five ways to pay, and each has its own cost.

  • Online or by phone through Paymentus (1-844-797-9075): cards carry a 2.29% convenience fee, Visa debit a $2.95 fee, and a bank transfer $0.35. Each transaction is capped at $100,000.
  • In person at the Administration Center in Hastings, the Northern Service Center in West St. Paul, or the Western Service Center in Apple Valley, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. weekdays, with a 2.49% fee on cards.
  • By mail to Property Taxation & Records, Attn: Taxation, 1590 Highway 55, Hastings, MN 55033-2343.
  • Automatic withdrawal, free, for owners whose lender does not pay the tax and who have no overdue tax. Forms filed now apply to taxes due in 2027, and a cancellation is due 15 days before a due date.

You can look up what you owe in the Property Information Search by entering only your house number.

What happens when Dakota County taxes go unpaid?

Tax unpaid on January 2 becomes delinquent and monthly interest is added. A judgment, which is a tax lien, is entered against the property, owners get a letter in March, and a list of delinquent parcels is published in a local newspaper for two weeks.

The owner then has three years to pay in full or set up a payment plan. If the balance is still open after that, the property forfeits to the State of Minnesota, and the county manages it for the state. For parcels with 2022 or earlier tax unpaid, the sheriff served notice in June 2026 and the pay-or-plan date was August 31, 2026.

Penalty abatement is possible but narrow. The county considers clerical error, hardship such as a death or serious illness, a government-declared emergency, a postal error admitted in writing, and a stop-payment on a lost check made within 30 days. It does not accept a missing statement, a late payment alone, or general financial hardship.

How do you appeal a Dakota County value?

For 2026 values the informal route and the county board are closed. The Special County Board of Appeal and Equalization met June 8, 2026, and after it adjourned Assessing Services could no longer change a 2026 value, so any change now applies to the 2027 assessment for taxes payable in 2028.

A petition to the Minnesota Tax Court is the formal option left. Section 278.01 requires a copy to be served on the county auditor and the petition and proof of service filed with the court administrator by April 30 of the year the tax is payable. Dakota County accepts email service at taxpetitions@co.dakota.mn.us, and it advises filing early because the county emails back an acknowledgment that must be filed with the court. Bring recent appraisals or sales of similar homes as evidence, and call the Tax Court at 651-539-3260 with questions.

Which Dakota County relief programs have filing dates?

The county's Home and Property page groups its relief programs together, and its 2026 date list gives a deadline for most of them. Missing one usually means waiting a full year.

  • Homestead, for owners who live in the house, with applications due December 31, 2026.
  • Blind and disabled homestead (Class 1b), due October 1.
  • Green Acres, due May 1, and Agricultural Preserves, due June 1.
  • Senior citizen property tax deferment, disabled veterans, open spaces and property tax exemption, plus state property tax refunds and local option disaster abatement.

The 2026 open book appeal ran March 11 to May 1, and manufactured home homestead applications were due May 29. The county also posts proposed taxes for 2027 on its Home and Property page.

What does the tax do at a Dakota County closing?

The county notes that cities and townships set their own sale rules, especially for wells, septic systems, manufactured homes and owners on Medical Assistance, whose certificate of clearance line is 651-554-6555. Under section 272.12, the county auditor must confirm there is no delinquent tax before a deed is recorded, and Dakota County says it can return a deed for delinquent tax.

Home buyers should also watch the calendar for programs. Homestead applications are due December 31, 2026, and the Blind or Disabled Class 1b applications were due October 1. Open Space applications are due November 3.

More questions about Dakota County, MN Property Tax Guide

What is the next Dakota County property tax deadline?

November 16, 2026, for agricultural property and manufactured homes, since November 15 is a Sunday. Real property was due May 15 and October 15. Homestead applications are due December 31.

Can I still appeal my 2026 Dakota County value?

Only through the Minnesota Tax Court. The county board met on June 8, 2026, so Assessing Services can change only the 2027 assessment. A petition for taxes payable in 2027 is due by April 30, 2027.

How do I pay Dakota County property tax by phone?

Call 1-844-797-9075 and use a Discover, MasterCard or Visa card at 2.29%, a Visa debit at $2.95, or a bank transfer at $0.35. Your payment is complete only once you get a confirmation number.

How long before Dakota County can take a property for unpaid tax?

Owners have three years from the delinquency to pay or set up a payment plan before the property forfeits to the state. Interest builds monthly in that time. Call 651-438-4576 about your parcel.

Does Dakota County give a free way to check my balance?

Yes. The Property Information Search is free, and you enter only your house number to see what you owe. Property Taxation & Records can help at taxation@co.dakota.mn.us or 651-438-4576, and the county also offers a free paperless notice option that sends your statement by email.

Anoka County by the numbers

Which Anoka County office sends the tax bill?

Property Records & Taxation does it all under one roof, from valuation to collection. The office is in the Government Center at 2100 3rd Avenue, Anoka, MN 55303. Phone 763-323-5400 for tax questions, or write to proptax@anokacountymn.gov about a valuation. Counter service runs weekdays from opening at eight in the morning until half past four, holidays excepted.

The county's Taxation page adds that Anoka County prints the proposed tax statements for a long list of taxing bodies at once: the county itself, your city, the school district and the state, depending on where the parcel sits and what type of property it is. The bill you pay is a combination of all of those levies.

What is Anoka County like for a home seller?

Anoka County is bordered by Hennepin and Ramsey counties to the south. It has 446 square miles, with the Mississippi River along the southwestern boundary and the Rum River running south through the west. The terrain is low, rolling and wooded, and the lakes include Coon, Ham, Bunker and Centerville.

The county was organized by the Minnesota Territorial Legislature on May 23, 1857, out of parts of Ramsey and Benton counties. Its seat is the city of Anoka, a name from the Dakota word for "on both sides," a reference to the town's place on both banks of the Rum River. Twenty cities fall inside the county, among them Anoka, Blaine, Coon Rapids, Fridley, Columbia Heights, Andover, Ramsey, Lino Lakes and Ham Lake.

Census QuickFacts supplies these numbers:

  • 381,605 people in mid-2025, packed at 862.4 per square mile of land
  • 145,902 housing units, with 80.2% occupied by owners
  • Owned homes valued at a median $346,500 (2020 to 2024)
  • Rent of $1,464 at the median, and owners with a mortgage pay $1,949 monthly
  • 774 building permits in 2025, and a household income median of $101,869

Twenty cities and one township fill the county, and the valuation appeal route depends on which city a house is in.

How does Anoka County value and classify a home?

The assessor values property as of January 2 each year and mails a Notice of Valuation and Classification. The estimated market value on that notice reflects what the assessor thinks the property would sell for on the open market. The class records how the property is used.

On a homestead, the notice also shows a Homestead Market Value Exclusion. The county's explanation gives the formula: a maximum of $38,000 at a market value of $95,000, falling by nine percent of the value above $95,000, and disappearing at $517,200. A seller whose house is worth more than that gets no exclusion, and a buyer in that range will see the full taxable value.

The notice lists other adjustments too, including an exclusion for veterans with disabilities, deferrals under Green Acres, Rural Preserve and Open Space, and a platted vacant land deferral. Taxable market value is the figure after all of those. A separate line shows new improvement value, the assessor's estimate of additions made in the past five years.

Higher value does not automatically raise your bill. The county notes that taxes follow the annual levy and how your value moves compared with neighboring properties.

How do I appeal an Anoka County valuation?

The path depends on your city, and the county's notice page spells it out. Your valuation notice tells you which option applies.

  • In a city that holds its own Local Board of Appeal and Equalization, you must appear there first if you want to go on to the county board.
  • In an Open Book city, you can skip straight to the County Board of Appeal and Equalization in June.
  • Either way, the County Board of Appeal and Equalization is the next stop if the first step did not settle things.

For a first conversation about the number itself, the Taxation page lists proptax@anokacountymn.gov and 763-323-5400. Have your parcel identification number ready.

Beyond the boards, Minnesota Statutes 278.01 lets an owner petition district court or the Tax Court by serving the county auditor, with proof of service filed by April 30 of the year the tax is payable. Statute 274.01 keeps local board meetings between April 1 and May 31.

How can I pay Anoka County property tax?

You can pay four ways, and the county sets out the costs for each. Taxes can be paid at PayAnokaCounty online, by mail, at the Government Center, or through a free automatic direct payment program.

Anoka County payment methods and what each costs (county Payment Options page)
MethodCostNotes
Online card, Apple Pay, Google Pay2.6% feeFee goes to the processor, not the county
Online eCheck$3.50Taken online only
Mail a checkNonePostmark must meet the due date; allow 2 weeks to post
In personNone for cash or check2.6% for cards; drop box available
Direct paymentFreePre-registration required; call 763-323-5400

The county warns that mail is sometimes not postmarked on the day it is dropped off. If the deadline is close, ask the post office counter for a hand-applied postmark, which is free. There is no grace period, and a due date that falls on a weekend moves to the first business day after the weekend. Payment due dates depend on how the property is classified.

When do Anoka County proposed tax statements arrive?

They are mailed in mid-November. The county calls them proposed 2027 property tax statements, and they are not final until the taxing bodies approve their levies in December. The county has posted budget and levy hearing dates on its Taxation page, and eNotices let an owner get the statement by email with the code printed on the proposed notice.

The county names four factors that move a bill: local levies from the city, school district and county, changes in the overall tax base, changes in your assessed value, and how your value change compares with others nearby. Hearings are for budgets, not valuations. The county says the Truth in Taxation meeting is not the place to argue your taxable market value.

The county also reports that in 2026 the legislature created a one-time increase of nearly 15% for homeowners who qualified for the 2025 regular property tax refund, with form M1PR due by August 15, 2027.

Who receives the Anoka County tax statement after I sell?

Often it is still you. Anoka County mails one statement per parcel a year, in mid-March, and a change in recorded ownership after January 1 does not trigger a new mailing. The statement goes to the previous owner or taxpayer, so a buyer and seller should plan for a duplicate request after closing.

A sale, a refinance or a mortgage satisfaction are the usual reasons for a different taxpayer, and each calls for a duplicate. Call 763-323-5400 if you have not received a statement by April 1. Not receiving one does not forgive the penalty or interest.

A manufactured home is taxed on a separate schedule, with statements mailed in July, and its title cannot be transferred until all current and delinquent personal property taxes are paid.

Which Carver County offices deal with property tax?

Two Carver County offices share the work, and both sit at 600 East 4th Street in Chaska. Billing and payments go through Property Tax at (952) 361-1910 or custsvc@carvercountymn.gov. Value, classification and homestead questions go to Property Assessment & Homesteading at (952) 361-1960 or assessment@carvercountymn.gov. The building keeps weekday hours of 8:00am to 4:30pm and is closed on government holidays.

The county mails tax statements each year by March 31. A statement that never shows up is no defense against penalty, a point the county's penalty page repeats in bold type.

When are Carver County property taxes due?

On most parcels the first installment falls on May 15 and the second on October 15. Most agricultural property pays its second half on November 15, and manufactured homes pay on August 31 and November 15. State law in Minn. Stat. 279.01 phrases the same dates as payment before May 16 and before October 16.

  • If the statement was not postmarked before April 25, the first-half deadline moves to 21 days past the postmark.
  • A parcel with $100 or less in tax pays the whole amount by the first-half date.
  • Class 4c seasonal recreational property not used commercially takes the homestead penalty schedule.
  • Second-half agricultural property pays no penalty if it is in by November 15.

There is only one statement. The second-half stub is on it, and the county does not mail another in the fall.

What penalty rates apply after a missed Carver County deadline?

Penalty begins the next day and climbs on the first day of every month. The county's schedule runs from 2% to 14%, and the numbers below are for a first-half payment on a residential parcel.

First-half penalty by payment date, Carver County residential property
Paid on or afterHomesteadNon-homestead
May 162%4%
June 14%8%
July 15%9%
August 16%10%
September 17%11%
October 18%12%
January 210%14%

Source: Carver County Penalty Rates page. First-half tax must be paid with its penalty before money counts toward the second half.

  • Only a U.S. Postal Service postmark by the due date counts. Private postage meter marks are rejected.
  • A bank bill-pay check usually carries no postmark, so it must arrive by the due date.
  • Online payments cannot come from a savings account, and a mistyped parcel number can delay a payment into penalty.

Minnesota also gives a one-time break: if a mailed payment is postmarked within one business day after the due date and the owner has not used the break before, the treasurer must abate the penalty (279.01, subd. 2).

How do I contest my Carver County valuation?

Start with a call to the assessor. The county lists four steps: contact the assessment office, attend an open book session or a local board, take the matter to the county board, and finally petition Minnesota Tax Court. You may file with the Tax Court directly at any point.

  1. January 2: every parcel is valued as of this date. The 2026 valuation, used for taxes payable in 2027, rests on sales from October 1, 2024 through September 30, 2025.
  2. March: the tax statement and the Notice of Valuation and Classification arrive together.
  3. April and May: local boards meet. State law sets those meetings between April 1 and May 31, and each board must finish within 20 days (Minn. Stat. 274.01). A board may not cut the assessor's total by more than one percent.
  4. June: the county board meets. You can appear only if you attended the local board, and you need an appointment made before June 1.
  5. April 30: Tax Court filing deadline. The 2026 date has passed, so the next one for the 2026 valuation is April 30, 2027.

In November every city, township, school district and the county hold Truth in Taxation meetings. Their notices show this year's tax and an estimate for the following year.

How do I pay Carver County property tax?

The county takes mailed checks, bank bill pay and an online payment system, and its penalty page gives the pitfalls to avoid. A check mailed on the due date needs a U.S. postmark from that day, and a bill-pay payment is on time only if it reaches the county by the due date. Re-enter the parcel number carefully, since a keying error can push a payment past the deadline. The payment portal does not accept a savings account.

Call (952) 361-1910 with questions about what is owed or how penalty is calculated. The county asks that first-half tax be paid in full, with any penalty, before money is applied to the second half.

What changes for property tax when a Carver County house sells?

Check the closing papers for who pays the year's tax, and confirm the full year is paid. The county's public access page shows statement copies and offers email reminders. For a payoff figure on anything past due, call (952) 361-1910.

Homestead status does not travel with the house. A new owner, a move into a trust, a name change or an owner added or removed each requires a new application to the assessor. Under 272.115 the assessor drops the homestead classification for the next assessment year after a sale unless the buyer applies and qualifies, and a buyer cannot be classed homestead if no certificate of value was filed. A qualifying owner may get the homestead market value exclusion, which lowers taxable value.

A seller whose taxes are behind can still sell. Ask the closing agent to request the amount due from the property tax office before the closing date, since penalty rises monthly.

Carver County covers 354 square miles of land, which makes it Minnesota's second-smallest county by that measure. Residents numbered 91,042 in 2010 and 106,922 in 2020, and the July 2025 estimate stands at 114,379. Chaska serves as seat of government and is the biggest city. Chanhassen lies partly in Hennepin County, so confirm which county bills a Chanhassen parcel before you call.

  • Households: 41,175, with 2.65 people each
  • Median household income: $125,946
  • Housing units, July 2025: 44,930

At the median value, each 1% of assessed value is about $4,536, so the March notice is worth reading line by line. The date of your local board meeting is printed on that notice.

May 15 for most properties. A statement mailed after April 24 pushes that date to 21 days after the postmark. The October installment falls on October 15, or on November 15 for most agricultural land.

Call the Carver County assessor at (952) 361-1960 or write to assessment@carvercountymn.gov. The assessor can explain the valuation notice and tell you the board dates for your city or township.

Is it too late to challenge the 2026 Carver County value?

The local and county board windows for 2026 and the April 30, 2026 Tax Court deadline have passed. Valuation notices for the next cycle arrive in March, and the next Tax Court filing deadline is April 30, 2027.

Penalty begins the next day. If the envelope carries a U.S. postmark within one business day of the deadline and you have never used the abatement before, state law lets the treasurer waive it.

Does the buyer keep my homestead on a Carver County house?

No. The assessor removes the homestead classification for the following assessment year unless the buyer files a homestead application and qualifies. The buyer applies through the assessor's office, and the county treats a new owner, a trust transfer or a name change as an event that needs a fresh application.

Which Chisago County office bills property tax?

The Auditor-Treasurer's Office in Center City calculates, bills and collects every property tax bill in Chisago County. It sits at 313 N Main Street, Room 271/274, and answers at 651-213-8500 from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Monday through Friday except holidays. Center City is also the county seat.

The same office handles property combinations and splits, records land transfers so names and addresses stay current, tracks special assessments, runs the tax forfeiture process and settles collected money with the local governments. Homestead applications and valuation questions go to the county assessor instead.

When do Chisago County statements arrive, and what if I never got one?

Real estate statements go out by March 31, and manufactured home statements by July 15. They also appear online one to two weeks after mailing. The statement is the only notice you get, and its two bottom stubs carry the first-half and second-half due dates.

Statement files are generated in mid-February for the owner of record at that moment. Anyone who bought later receives no statement, and the county still holds the owner responsible for knowing when taxes are due. Download a copy from the county's property tax page or call for one. The county adds that statements go to the owner whether or not a mortgage escrow account exists, and the owner must know whether the lender or the owner pays.

When is Chisago County property tax due?

Tax under $100 and all personal property is due in full on May 15. Larger bills may be paid in two installments, and the dates depend on the property class.

  • Real estate: May 15 and October 15
  • Agricultural: May 15 and November 15
  • Mobile home: August 31 and November 15
  • Personal property: May 15

Mailed payments count as on time only with a postmark on or before the due date. The county urges anyone paying near a deadline to take the envelope to the post office and ask the postmaster to postmark it.

How much penalty does a late second half carry in Chisago County?

The county publishes a separate table for each property type. This one covers the second-half payment on residential homestead and cabin property, plus the case where both halves are unpaid.

Source: Chisago County Due Dates & Penalties page. Non-homestead rates run higher: a first-half payment made after October 1 carries 12%, and 14% after January 2.

Penalty stops when a bill turns delinquent on the first business day of January. Interest then starts under Minn. Stat. 270.03 at 8% a year, charged as simple interest each month on the tax, penalty and publication fee.

What happens when Chisago County taxes go delinquent?

Taxes unpaid from a prior year are delinquent. By February 15 the county auditor files the delinquent list with the district court administrator, a step the county ties to Minn. Stat. 279.05. Minn. Stat. 279.09 then has the list published in the county's official newspaper by March 20, with a second printing at least two weeks later. Chisago County charges $25 per parcel to recover that cost.

  • Only full payment of all delinquent tax removes a parcel from the list.
  • Partial payments are encouraged because they cut the balance and the interest, but they do not stop forfeiture.
  • If the balance is not paid by the end of the redemption period, usually three years but it varies by class, the property can be forfeited.
  • Anyone near the end of that period should call the office to ask about options.

How do I get homestead status or sell a mobile home in Chisago County?

An owner who lives in the home as a primary residence, or whose qualifying relative lives there, applies to the county assessor on the Homestead Application. Completed forms are due by December 31, either in person or by mail. The county page also lists tracks for relative homestead, disabled veteran, manufactured home, special agricultural, blind or disabled (class 1b) and first-time home buyer. A spouse may claim a separate homestead in cases such as pending dissolution, legal separation or a job that keeps the spouse at least 50 miles away.

Moving or selling a mobile home takes a Tax Release Letter signed by the Auditor-Treasurer showing no tax owed. The seller must show a current title in the seller's name first, and the buyer takes both the title and the letter to a Minnesota motor vehicle office. The nearest is the Chisago City DMV.

How does the Chisago County appeal process work?

In March the assessor mails a Valuation and Classification Notice that lists market value, class, new improvements and exclusions such as homestead. Call the assessor first. Most Chisago County communities then hold a Local Board of Appeal and Equalization, and an owner who still disagrees may go to the County Board of Appeal and Equalization. You can appeal value and classification, but not the tax itself.

Every parcel is valued as of January 2, and appraisers visit each property about once every five years. For the January 2, 2026 assessment, the assessor used sales from October 1, 2024 through September 30, 2025, and each sale's Certificate of Real Estate Value helps separate open-market sales from bank-owned or family transfers. Under Minn. Stat. 274.01, an owner who was told of a proposed increase and neither appeared nor wrote to the local board cannot go on to the county board. For budget complaints, use the Truth in Taxation meetings or the annual township meeting.

Pull the current statement and confirm that both halves are paid or scheduled. The county site has an online property search for recent and prior years, an interactive GIS map, a property tax calculator and an address change form for statements. Updating the mailing address matters most after you sell, since the owner of record gets the next statement.

Check the class on your statement too. A homestead classification lowers tax, and the buyer will have to apply for it separately. Parcels with forfeited or delinquent history should be cleared first, because only full payment takes a parcel off the delinquent list. When in doubt, call 651-213-8500 and ask for the amount owed through a specific date.

Each city runs its own council, and the county posts each council's meeting schedule. Andersen Corporation, the window and door maker, is among the large manufacturers named for the county.

When are Chisago County property taxes due?

What if my Chisago County tax statement never came?

What interest does Chisago County charge on delinquent tax?

The office is open Monday through Friday, 8 am to 4:30 pm. Besides property tax, the department runs elections, vital statistics, licensing and the parcel mapping system.

Value and classification belong to the county assessor at (218) 547-7298. Cass uses one county-wide assessment system, so every parcel in every township is valued from the same office rather than by local assessors. The first half of real property tax is due May 15, and the non-farm second half is due October 15. Farm real property and manufactured homes pay their second half on November 15. A class 3a owner attaches an affidavit, and the county asks eligible businesses to return its Commercial Tax Deferral Form.

How can I pay a Cass County tax bill?

  • By mail to the Cass County Auditor-Treasurer with the right stub, postmarked before the due date. The second-half stub sits directly above the first-half stub at the bottom of the statement.

What is the Cass County refuse management fee?

Cass County charges a flat refuse management fee on improved parcels with an assessed value of at least $1,000. The charge began in 1990, was once called the solid waste fee, and funds waste disposal and recycling programs. The county board has kept it as a flat fee instead of folding the cost into the levy.

  • Commercial under $9,999 in building value: $86
  • Commercial from $10,000 to $99,999: $195
  • Commercial from $100,000 to $499,999: $391

Market value is set as of January 2 each year. The state expects an assessor's value to land between 90% and 105% of sale price, and the county says it has stayed within that range. File a homestead application with the assessor. The same office can tell blind or disabled owners and disabled veterans whether they qualify for the relief Minnesota offers them. The refund program for homeowners is run by the state, so Cass County staff direct those questions to the forms and instructions from the Department of Revenue.

Tell the Auditor-Treasurer your new mailing address as soon as you move. The county warns that a wrong address can delay or block time-sensitive statements and other property mailings, and care-of addresses can be added. It also says no owner name is changed in the tax records without a recorded legal document.

Sellers working through a contract for deed should read the county's Property Tax Billing and Collection Procedures fact sheet, which explains who receives the statement.

What happens to unpaid taxes and tax-forfeited land in Cass County?

Interest begins on unpaid balances after January 2 of the following year, and penalties and rates follow state statute. Partial payments are accepted on prior-year taxes, with a $100 minimum preferred. The money goes to the newest year first and then back through earlier years. The county states that nonpayment results in loss of the property through forfeiture under Minnesota law.

Cass County's Land Department manages about 255,000 acres of tax-forfeited land, with timber sales, reforestation and wildlife management on it. Call the Auditor-Treasurer at (218) 547-7260 for the amount past due on a parcel. If you sell on a contract for deed, only the new contract holder receives the bill, but the seller still has to watch that the taxes get paid.

Cass County is large and quiet: 2,022 square miles of land plus 393 of water, and a 2025 population estimate of 31,430. Walker holds the courthouse, and Lake Shore is the biggest city. Much of the Leech Lake Indian Reservation lies in the county, and Chippewa National Forest and Crow Wing State Park reach into it. Winters are cold: the Walker January average low is 0 degrees F.

The gap between 25,344 housing units and 12,874 households points to a large stock of seasonal and second homes, and the statute puts class 4c seasonal recreational property on the homestead penalty schedule. Anyone listing a lake cabin in a township such as Pine River, Shingobee or Boy Lake, should check the class on the statement and the payment dates that go with it.

It is the refuse management fee that applies to residential and seasonal parcels with an assessed value of at least $1,000. It pays for waste disposal and recycling in the county.

Who runs property tax in Crow Wing County?

One department, Land Services, both assesses and collects in Crow Wing County. You will find it at 322 Laurel Street in Brainerd, the seat of the county, and its phone line is 218-824-1010.

Land Services mails bills, takes payments, answers valuation questions and keeps the field books and parcel records that the public can research on the lower level of its building. The county's Property Search website shows parcel data, and a duplicate tax statement can be pulled there by parcel ID or address.

What should a seller know about Crow Wing County's housing stock?

This is lake country in east central Minnesota: 999 square miles of land, about 417 named lakes, the Mississippi cutting through, and gently rolling wooded ground. Census estimates for July 2025 show 69,132 residents, a gain of 4.6% since the 2020 base.

  • Communities on the county's list include Brainerd, Baxter, Crosby, Crosslake, Garrison, Nisswa, Pequot Lakes, Breezy Point, Deerwood and Fort Ripley.
  • The Census Bureau counts 44,306 housing units and 29,402 households, and Wikipedia's 2020 figures show 32.9% of housing units vacant, which points to a large stock of cabins.
  • Owners live in 77.0% of occupied homes, and the typical home among them is worth $306,800 (2020 to 2024).
  • A typical household earns $72,589, and 26.8% of residents have passed 65.
  • Builders took out 625 permits in 2025.

Brainerd began in 1870 when the Northern Pacific Railroad picked the site for its Mississippi River crossing, and it took the county seat from the earlier trading village of Crow Wing. Because so many parcels here are lakeshore, classification matters: a homestead and a seasonal cabin are taxed under different rules.

What are the Crow Wing County payment dates?

The first half of a real estate bill falls due May 15 and the second half October 15. Farmland gets until November 15 for its second half. Mobile homes are billed on August 31 and November 15.

Resorts and businesses that earn more than 60% of gross income between May and August can file an affidavit to push the first-half date to May 31, and the affidavit must accompany the payment. All 2026 real estate dates have now passed, so any balance from this year is already carrying penalty.

A bill unpaid on December 31 of its due year turns delinquent. For delinquent years, the county asks you to call Land Services at 218-824-1010 before paying so you pay the right amount, and it notes that payments are applied to the newest years first under Minnesota Statutes section 280.39.

How steep is the Crow Wing County late penalty?

Penalties come from a state-set table that the county posts, and an unpaid first half climbs the fastest. The county's own figures for that half are below.

Penalty on an unpaid first half, Crow Wing County Land Services table

Manufactured homes carry an 8% penalty from September 1 on the first half, and personal property is at 8% from May 16. State law also allows the treasurer to abate the penalty one time for a mailed check postmarked within a business day of the deadline.

Where and how can you pay in Crow Wing County?

Land Services accepts four kinds of payment.

  • Online: E-check costs $1.95 and a card costs 2.35% of the payment or $1.95, whichever is greater, with a $50,000 limit. The processor collects those fees, not the county, and credit takes three to four days to post.
  • You need the 8-digit parcel number for each parcel, and a full year is paid by choosing Pay Full Year.
  • At the counter: weekdays from eight in the morning to 4:30 in the afternoon, with an outside drop box that never closes.
  • By mail: send the remittance stub and payment to Land Services, 322 Laurel Street Ste 15, Brainerd, MN 56401.

How are Crow Wing values set, and how do you push back?

The office revalues every parcel yearly and must land between 90% and 105% of market value. Staff walk each property once in five years and check permits. Comparable sales drive the number, adjusted for land, size, quality and condition, and the class follows how the property is used today.

The county lays out two routes. Route one runs through the boards: a local board or open book meeting first, then the county board, which requires a call ahead to be placed on its agenda. A city or township with no local board sends owners to an open book session before the county board. Route two is the Minnesota Tax Court.

  • Meeting times and places are printed on your Notice of Valuation and Classification.
  • You may appear in person, send a letter, or use a representative you authorize.
  • A court petition has an April 30 filing date for the year the tax is payable (section 278.01).

Which tax relief programs does Crow Wing point to?

The county's Taxes page links to Minnesota Department of Revenue guidance for owners who may qualify for a lower bill. Several of them depend on filing before a deadline, so ask Land Services which ones fit your parcel.

  • Homestead classification and the homestead market value exclusion for owner-occupied houses.
  • Special homestead classification for owners who are blind or disabled.
  • Senior citizen property tax deferral.
  • Market value exclusion for veterans with a disability.
  • 2c managed forest land and the Sustainable Forest Incentive Act.
  • Green Acres and rural preserve deferral for agricultural and rural vacant land, plus special agricultural homestead.
  • Property tax refunds.

A seller who is behind on tax can also pay part of a bill. The treasurer may accept less than the full installment, and under section 279.01 the money goes to the oldest unpaid installment first. A payment that falls short is applied to accrued penalty before tax. A partial payment does not waive the minimum payment needed to keep an appeal alive.

How does a Crow Wing sale treat unpaid tax?

Delinquent tax blocks recording: the auditor has to clear the land first (section 272.12). A sale over $3,000 also brings a certificate of real estate value (section 272.115), and the seller's homestead class drops off until the buyer applies and qualifies.

Ask Land Services for a payoff figure for each parcel, since a lake property sale often includes several. The assessing office also lists tax relief programs that can matter to a new owner, such as 2c managed forest, disabled veterans, Green Acres, homesteading and rural preserve.

Where do I pay Crow Wing County property taxes?

You pay Land Services at 322 Laurel Street Ste 15 in Brainerd, online, by mail or in a drop box. The counter is open Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and the phone is 218-824-1010.

What are the Crow Wing County due dates?

Real estate is due May 15 and October 15, agricultural second half on November 15, and mobile homes on August 31 and November 15. The 2026 real estate dates have passed, so the next one is the first half in May 2027.

How much is the late penalty on a Crow Wing County homestead?

It starts at 2% on an unpaid first half after May 15 and reaches 8% by October 1, according to the county's table. Non-homestead property starts at 4% and tops out at 12%.

Can I challenge my Crow Wing County valuation now?

The local and county board meetings for the 2026 value are finished. A Tax Court or district court petition on taxes payable in 2027 is due April 30, 2027, so call Land Services at 218-824-1010 and ask for the assessor.

Do delinquent Crow Wing County taxes need to be paid before a sale?

Yes, delinquent taxes must be cleared before the deed can be recorded. Call Land Services at 218-824-1010 before paying them online, because the county wants staff to confirm the right amount and avoid extra penalty. Delinquent years can also be paid in person or by check or money order after that call.

Goodhue County by the numbers

What is Goodhue County like for a home seller?

Goodhue County sits in southeastern Minnesota on the Wisconsin border, across Lake Pepin, with Red Wing as the county seat. The legislature carved it out of Wabasha County on March 5, 1853, and it was named for James Madison Goodhue, who published the first newspaper in the territory. Wheat built the early economy, and for several years the county led the country in wheat output. Today the ground is rolling hills and bluffs cut by the Cannon River, and traffic runs on U.S. 52, 61 and 63.

Census QuickFacts gives a picture of the housing a seller is dealing with:

  • 48,195 residents in the July 2025 estimate, up 1.3% since the 2020 census.
  • 19,727 households, with 78.8% of homes lived in by their owners.
  • A median owner-occupied home value of $285,100 and a median household income of $84,171.
  • 84 building permits in 2025 across 21,445 housing units.

Cities include Red Wing, Cannon Falls, Zumbrota, Kenyon, Wanamingo, Goodhue and pieces of Lake City and Pine Island. Red Wing Public Schools, Cannon Falls, Zumbrota-Mazeppa and Kenyon-Wanamingo are among the school districts that levy on county homes.

Which Goodhue County office handles property tax?

Finance and Taxpayer Services runs both the assessor and the auditor/treasurer from the second floor of the Government Center, 509 W. 5th St. in Red Wing. The phone is 651-385-3040 and the counter is open Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. For assessor questions, choose option 1.

The county reminds owners that its board controls only the county budget and levy. Of thirteen reasons a bill can move, which include a change in your value, a shift in other owners' values, city or township levies, school levies, referendums, special assessments and state aid or law changes, only the county piece belongs to the commissioners. A seller who sees a jump should check which piece moved before calling.

When are Goodhue County property taxes due?

Minnesota Statutes 279.01 splits the bill into two halves, payable before May 16 and before October 16 when the tax on a parcel is over $100. Agricultural homestead and qualifying farm land may pay the second half without penalty through November 15.

Penalty starts at 2 percent on homestead and 4 percent on nonhomestead on the day after a due date. It is repeated on the first of the next month, then 1 percent monthly through December, topping out at 8 percent for homestead and 12 percent for nonhomestead. The treasurer must abate a late penalty once if the envelope was postmarked within one business day of the due date and the owner has not used that abatement before.

Owners can search records and pay from the Finance page link labeled Search Property Tax Records/Pay Property Tax, and the office can quote a payoff for a parcel before closing.

How does Goodhue County arrive at my value?

The assessor estimates market value and classification for more than 29,000 parcels as of January 2, and the figure sets taxes payable the following year. Staff try to view the inside and outside of each home, list size, age, quality, basement finish and extras, and feed that into a mass appraisal system that a county appraiser reviews. Sales from October 1 through September 30 before the assessment date are the guide.

State rules require every property to be physically reviewed at least once every five years and require the overall level of assessment to land between 90 and 105 percent of market value. The county says it consistently meets that test. Classification matters as much as value: homestead, nonhomestead residential, apartment and commercial are each taxed at a percentage set by the legislature. The county is also doing on-site reassessments in several areas during 2026, so a seller whose neighborhood is on that list should expect a visit request.

Do values and rules differ across Goodhue County?

They can. The county spans ten cities, either whole or in part, and 21 townships, and each has its own levy on top of the county and school district levies. A house in Red Wing and a farmhouse in Vasa Township share a county assessor, yet they face different local boards, different school districts and sometimes different reassessment schedules. Part of the county touches Dakota County to the northwest and Olmsted to the southeast, and Prairie Island Indian Community lies almost entirely within the county.

The assessor's notice for 2026 says on-site reassessments are under way in a number of areas. If you get a letter asking for an interior viewing, answering it gives the appraiser accurate facts about finish, condition and extras, which is easier than arguing about them after the notice arrives. The county adds that owners who think the value and classification on their notice are right do not need to contact the assessor at all.

How do I appeal a Goodhue County assessment?

Start with facts. Pull recent sales of comparable homes and any market analysis, then call the assessor at 651-385-3040 option 1 and walk an appraiser through them. An interior inspection can be scheduled. If the question is still open, go to the local board of appeal and equalization, then make an appointment with the county board. The county board listing shows a June 15 meeting by appointment only, and the call to book it goes through the same number.

Goodhue County appeal path, from the county assessor's appeal page
StepWhereDetail
1AssessorGather sales, call 651-385-3040 option 1, review with an appraiser
2Interior inspectionSchedule if the appraiser asks
3Local boardAttend the meeting for your city or township
4County boardAppointment only, 509 W. 5th St., Red Wing
5Minnesota Tax CourtPhone 651-539-3260; filing deadline April 30

Only the current year valuation can go through the boards. The county says an appeal of a prior year value runs through Tax Court alone, and Statutes 278.01 sets April 30 of the tax year as the court filing date.

What should I check in Goodhue County before listing?

  • The valuation notice mailed in March, for the estimated market value and the class assigned to the home.
  • Whether the home is still classified as homestead for the owner who is selling.
  • Whether the neighborhood is in the 2026 reassessment group.
  • Both halves of the current year tax, and any older balance on the parcel.
  • Whether any appeal is pending, since Tax Court filings for a tax year close on April 30.

Finance and Taxpayer Services can answer the tax and assessor items at 651-385-3040, and the title company handles the payoff once a buyer is under contract.

What happens to the tax bill when I sell a Goodhue County house?

Delinquent tax comes first. Under Minnesota Statutes 272.12 the auditor checks a deed for delinquent tax before transfer, and the recorder will not file it without the auditor's note. If the sale covers only part of a parcel, Statutes 272.121 calls for the treasurer's certification that the full-parcel tax for the current year is paid.

For an ordinary whole-parcel sale, ask the title company how this year's first and second halves will be split, and ask Finance and Taxpayer Services for the amount still open on the parcel. Buyers who plan to live in the home should apply for homestead; the county assessor's notice says people who bought or moved into a property in the past year may qualify for a property tax refund.

More questions about Goodhue County, MN Property Tax Guide

Who sets property values in Goodhue County?

The county assessor, working from the Government Center in Red Wing. Values are set as of January 2 and mailed to owners in March. Call 651-385-3040 option 1 with questions.

When is the Goodhue County board of appeal and equalization?

The county page lists June 15, by appointment only. Call 651-385-3040 option 1 to book a time before then, after trying the local board for your city or township.

Can I appeal last year's Goodhue County value?

Only through Minnesota Tax Court. The county says prior year values cannot go to its boards, and the court filing must be made by April 30 of the year the taxes are due.

What are the Goodhue County tax due dates?

Half is due before May 16 and half before October 16, per Minnesota Statutes 279.01. Qualifying agricultural property can pay the second half by November 15 without penalty.

Do I need to pay delinquent tax to sell my Goodhue County home?

Yes. A deed cannot be recorded until the auditor certifies no delinquent tax remains, so the payoff is normally handled at closing by the title company.

Who runs property tax in Aitkin County?

Responsibility is split. One office sets the value and class of each parcel, and another sends the bills and takes payment. The Assessor's Office answers at 218-927-7327. The Treasurer is at 307 2nd St NW, Room 119, Aitkin, MN 56431, and takes calls at 218-927-7325.

The Assessor's page says market value and classification are the main inputs to a tax bill, and that the office works under Minnesota statutes, Department of Revenue directives and County Board directives. A free parcel viewer called LINK shows basic parcel data. More detailed building records, including dimensions and sales reports, need a paid subscription, which the Assessor can explain by phone.

A seller here will end up talking to both: the Assessor about value and class, and the Treasurer about any balance on the parcel before the deed is signed.

What does the Aitkin County housing market look like?

Aitkin County sits in east central Minnesota and its seat is the city of Aitkin. Total area is 1,995 square miles, with 174 of them water. The Mississippi River flows south through the west central part, the terrain is wooded rolling hills, and Savanna Portage State Park and Rice Lake National Wildlife Refuge are among the protected areas on the map.

The first version of the county dates to 1857, when it carried the name Aiken, and the current spelling came in 1872. Its namesake, William Alexander Aitken, traded furs for the American Fur Company, and local government was organized in 1871. January lows in the city of Aitkin average about 0 degrees Fahrenheit, with a recorded extreme of minus 47 in 1972.

Census QuickFacts figures worth knowing before you price a house here:

  • Population of 16,252 as of July 2025, about 8.6 people per square mile of land
  • 14,681 housing units, 85.3% lived in by their owners
  • Median value of an owned home: $255,800 (2020 to 2024 survey years)
  • Households earn a median $60,833, and 35.7% of residents are past 65
  • 214 building permits in 2025, plus a 27.7 minute average drive to work

Owners dominate, and the older age profile is worth keeping in mind if the house you are selling belonged to a relative.

Is Aitkin County inspecting properties for 2027?

Yes, in a set of areas. A 2027 reassessment is listed on the Assessor's page, with appraisers on the road since May 2026. An inspection can land anywhere from May 2026 to February 2027, so one may still be ahead.

The areas on the list are Ball Bluff, Balsam, Fleming, Hazelton, Jevne, Macville, Malmo and Turner townships, unorganized territories 51-22, 52-24 and 52-25, and the city of Hill City. The county explains that this is a physical inspection used to check and fix its records, and that state law calls for it on all taxable property at least every five years.

Owners who want to be there for the walk-through can phone 218-927-7327, and the office also asks to hear about any hazards to avoid on the land. Keep receipts for recent repairs handy if you are in one of these areas.

How do I appeal an Aitkin County valuation or classification?

The county's appeals page sets a sequence, and the first step is a phone call:

  • Contact the Assessor's Office and have the front and back of your valuation notice in front of you.
  • Next comes the local board of appeal, staffed by the township board or city council, or an Open Book session if that is what your notice lists. At Open Book, the assessors review the case and decide, and that decision can still go to the county board.
  • After that is the county board, which meets in June. You schedule a time through the County Assessor, and the local step comes first unless your area has no local board.
  • The last stop is the Minnesota Tax Court, which the county says accepts petitions even from owners who skipped the earlier steps. Its deadline is April 30 of the taxes-payable year.

Statute 274.01 puts local board meetings in April and May and caps their combined reductions at one percent of the assessor's total. Under 278.01, an owner may instead serve a petition on the county auditor and file it in district court.

What are the Aitkin County tax due dates?

Bills come in two installments, one in mid-May and one in mid-October. These are the points that matter for an Aitkin County parcel:

Payment rules for Aitkin County parcels (Treasurer FAQ and Statute 279.01)
ItemWhat applies
First halfDue before May 16
Second halfDue before October 16, with no second-half statement mailed
Mailed paymentOn time when the postmark shows the due date or earlier
Late penalty after the due date2% on homestead, 4% on nonhomestead
Delinquent statusTax still unpaid when the new year begins
Delinquent listPrinted in the newspaper each March

The Treasurer does not mail second-half statements, so keep the stub from the first one. Missing paperwork is no defense: the office says the owner is still responsible, and courtesy letters for unpaid current-year tax carry added penalty and fees. After the first jump, the statute adds one percent per month, up to 8% on homestead and 12% on nonhomestead land.

Under the same statute, a tax of $100 or less is due in one payment with the first half. Owners of small parcels should ask the Treasurer which threshold applies before paying.

Who pays what when an Aitkin County house sells?

On this point the Treasurer's FAQ is direct: delinquent taxes get paid at closing. The closing statement, or the realtor or attorney on the deal, will show how the current year is divided.

Escrow customers have a lender that receives the figures straight from the county. The copy mailed to the owner says in bold print not to pay, yet it remains useful at filing time and for refund claims. A buyer who closes after statements went out can get a copy online or from the Treasurer, and the county says that is the buyer's job.

Two state rules touch the deed itself. Statute 272.115 requires a certificate of value on sales above $3,000 and has the assessor remove homestead status after a sale unless the buyer applies and qualifies. Statute 287.21 sets the deed tax at 0.33% of net consideration above that figure.

A mobile home is handled separately. Its title cannot move until the taxes are paid, and relocating one takes a Mobile Home Clearance Sheet from the Treasurer.

Can Aitkin County homeowners get tax relief?

Two programs appear in the Treasurer's FAQ. The state property tax refund is claimed on form M1PR, available from the Department of Revenue.

The second is the Senior Citizen Property Tax Deferral. The county calls it a low-interest loan from the state and says it is not tax forgiveness. Homeowners aged 65 or older with household income of $60,000 or less can defer part of the tax, the state pays the county, and interest accrues. A seller already in the program should ask the Department of Revenue how a sale affects the deferred balance before listing.

If you cannot tell whether either program fits, the Treasurer at 218-927-7325 can say what to bring.

More questions about Aitkin County, MN Property Tax Guide

Which office answers questions on an Aitkin County tax bill?

The Treasurer, at 218-927-7325, handles billing, payments and statement copies, from an office at 307 2nd St NW, Room 119. For value or class questions, dial the Assessor at 218-927-7327.

Does Aitkin County accept mailed tax payments?

Yes. A payment counts as timely if the postmark meets the due date. Address it to the Treasurer at 307 2nd St NW, Room 119, Aitkin, MN 56431. The back of each stub has a form for changing the mailing address.

What if my Aitkin County tax statement never arrives?

You still owe the tax and the same penalties apply. A replacement copy can be printed online or requested from the Treasurer.

Must back taxes be cleared to close an Aitkin County sale?

Yes, delinquent taxes are paid at closing. Tax left unpaid into the next calendar year is delinquent, so ask the Treasurer for a payoff amount well ahead of the closing date.

Is there a way to contest value after the spring boards adjourn?

Yes, by petitioning the Minnesota Tax Court before April 30 of the taxes-payable year. The Assessor's appeals page says the court hears owners who never went to the local or county board.

Which Becker County offices run property tax?

Becker County divides the job between the Assessor and the Auditor-Treasurer. The Assessor is appointed by the County Board of Commissioners and approved by the Minnesota Commissioner of Revenue. That office supervises the assessments of every township and city in the county and keeps records on about 29,200 taxable properties and 3,339 tax-exempt ones.

Appraisal work is done by state accredited and certified staff from the county office, along with certified assessors hired by townships and cities. The county supplies value and classification schedules built from sales ratio studies, which the Assessor uses to equalize values between properties, taxing districts, school districts and neighboring counties.

The Auditor-Treasurer, an elected official, calculates rates, prepares statements and Truth in Taxation notices, collects the tax and county special assessments, and tracks unpaid parcels. Most Assessor records are public, apart from data covered by the privacy act.

What is the Becker County housing market like?

Becker County lies in northwest Minnesota, with Detroit Lakes as the county seat. It covers 1,445 square miles, of which 130 are water, making it the 15th largest Minnesota county by area. Several hundred lakes, farmland and forest share the landscape, among them Detroit Lake, Lake Sallie, Lake Maud, Lake Melissa and Big Cormorant Lake. The highest point is a hill near Wolf Lake at 1,861 feet.

The county was created on March 18, 1858 and organized in 1871. It carries the name of George Loomis Becker, one of three men elected to Congress at statehood. Minnesota could send only two, so Becker stayed behind and was promised a county. Colonel George Johnston founded Detroit Lakes in 1871 and the Northern Pacific Railroad fueled its early growth. An 1877 vote made Detroit the seat over Frazee, Lake Park and Audubon, and the Soo Line built through the county in 1903.

Census QuickFacts for the housing market:

  • 35,497 residents in July 2025, with 26.8 people per square mile of land
  • 20,440 housing units, and 77.2% of homes lived in by the owner
  • Median value of $291,000 for an owned home, with median rent at $920
  • Monthly owner costs of $1,691 with a mortgage and $580 without
  • 182 building permits in 2025, and retail sales of $21,864 per person in 2022

One in four residents is 65 or older, and 7.2% identify as American Indian or Alaska Native, and White Earth is among the county's census-designated places.

What does the Becker County assessment calendar look like?

The Assessor's timeline page lists duties through the year. The dates below are the ones a homeowner is most likely to need.

  • January 2 is the assessment date for real and personal property.
  • February 1 is the last day to file for exemption from taxation.
  • March 31: statements go out by this date from the Treasurer, except for manufactured homes.
  • April 1 to May 31: local boards of appeal and equalization hold their meetings, and value notices go out at least ten days ahead.
  • April 30: last day to file a Tax Court petition about current taxes.
  • June: the County Board of Appeal and Equalization meets during the last ten meeting days after the second Friday, with times printed on the valuation notice.
  • August 15: deadline for the Property Tax Refund, Form M-1PR.
  • Late November: Truth in Taxation notices go out, with public hearings in the weeks after.

December 1 is the last day for owners of real property to establish homestead for the year, though applications can be filed with the Assessor until December 15 to count for that year's assessment.

When are Becker County property taxes due?

Most owners pay in two installments, May 15 and October 15, but the county's own schedule lists several exceptions that depend on property class.

Becker County schedule of property taxes payable, by class and date (Auditor-Treasurer schedule)
DateWho it covers
May 15First half of real property tax; personal property tax
May 31First half for class 1c and 4c resorts and qualifying class 3a seasonal commercial property
August 31First half of manufactured home personal property tax
October 15Second half for non-farm real property
November 15Second half for farm real property and for manufactured homes

Statute 279.01 adds two details. When the statements miss an April 25 postmark, the first installment moves to 21 days after the postmark date. Class 3a seasonal property qualifies for the later date only if the owner attaches an affidavit showing more than 60 percent of gross income comes from May through August.

A homestead owner on federal active service as a National Guard or reserve member gets four extra months, moving a May 15 payment to September 15 and an October 15 payment to February 15, with a copy of orders or form DD214.

How do I pay Becker County property tax online?

The Auditor-Treasurer's page links to an online and phone payment service, and e-check or card payments through it carry extra fees. The county asks for specific identifiers so the payment is credited to the right parcel.

  • Bill number: five digits, leaving off the beginning zero, printed on the first-half and second-half stubs.
  • Parcel or property ID: all nine digits with no decimal points, so 01.0001.000 is entered as 010001000.
  • Jurisdiction code: 3308 identifies Becker County.

The same page offers a parcel and tax record search showing taxes, assessments, and land and building features, linked to the county's online mapping. Run it before you list to review the taxes and assessments on record for your parcel.

What is the Becker County appeal route?

Begin with the Assessor, because a conversation about the value notice often resolves a data error. If it does not, the local board is the next step. Statute 274.01 makes the town board or city council the local board unless the city has a charter board or has handed the job to the county. Someone who ignores a notice that the board plans to raise the assessment generally cannot go to the county board later.

The county board convenes in June. After that, a petition to district court or Tax Court under Statute 278.01 must be on file by April 30 of the taxes-payable year. Appeals of manufactured homes assessed as personal property run on a separate calendar, with a September 1 petition date.

What happens to Becker County taxes when I sell?

The Auditor-Treasurer touches the sale before the Recorder does. That office collects the state deed tax, mortgage registration tax and split fees on conveyances and enters each transfer in a permanent database before the document is filed with the County Recorder. Questions on the electronic certificate of real estate value go to the Assessor's chief deputy.

Unpaid tax carries consequences beyond penalties. The Auditor-Treasurer puts delinquent parcels into judgment, runs forfeiture proceedings and sales under statute, and may use revenue recapture to collect. A seller with a back balance should settle it before closing instead of leaving it for the buyer's title company to find.

A few programs affect timing. Senior citizens apply for the state's property tax deferral by July 1 for taxes payable the following year, and farmland owners file for Green Acres deferral by May 1. Resort owners declare class 1c or 4c status with the Assessor by January 15, and people who are blind or permanently and totally disabled apply to the Department of Revenue for the special homestead class by October 1.

More questions about Becker County, MN Property Tax Guide

Who is the Becker County Assessor appointed by?

The County Board of Commissioners appoints the Assessor, and the Minnesota Commissioner of Revenue approves the appointment. The office supervises assessments for all townships and cities in the county.

When is the second Becker County property tax payment due?

October 15 for non-farm real property. Second-half tax on farm real property, including split-class parcels that are partly agricultural, is due November 15, as is the second half for manufactured homes.

Do Becker County resorts pay property tax on a different date?

Yes, the schedule differs for them. Class 1c and 4c resort property and qualifying class 3a seasonal commercial property may pay the first half by May 31 instead of May 15, per the county schedule and Statute 279.01.

What do I need to pay Becker County taxes online?

You need the five-digit bill number from your payment stub, the nine-digit parcel number without decimal points, and the jurisdiction code 3308. E-check and card payments add fees.

Where do I send questions about a Becker County eCRV?

Contact the Chief-Deputy Assessor, who the county lists for tax estimates, agricultural questions and eCRV inquiries. The County Assessor handles exempt questions and sales inquiries.

What should a seller know about Hubbard County?

Hubbard County is in northwestern Minnesota, with Park Rapids as the seat. It was created on February 26, 1883 from part of Cass County and named for Lucius Hubbard, governor from 1882 to 1887. The land is hilly, wooded and dotted with lakes, and parts of Itasca State Park, the Mississippi Headwaters and the Leech Lake Indian Reservation fall inside the county line. The cities are Akeley, Laporte, Nevis and Park Rapids.

The numbers from Census QuickFacts explain why property tax here looks different from the metro:

  • 22,369 residents in the July 2025 estimate, up 4.8% from the 2020 base.
  • 14,900 housing units but only 8,964 households, so a large share of homes are not a full-time residence. The 2020 census counted 39.6% of housing units as vacant.
  • 83.1% owner occupancy, a median home value of $282,600 and a median household income of $71,995.
  • 28.5% of residents are 65 or older.

A cabin or lake home that is used for part of the year is taxed differently from a primary residence, which is why classification is the first thing to check before listing.

Which Hubbard County office handles property tax?

Two departments share the work. The Auditor/Treasurer is responsible for property tax administration, delinquent taxes and the published delinquent tax list, and for forfeitures, repurchases and confessions of judgment. By statute the auditor also sits on the county board of equalization.

The assessor operates inside Property Records at the Government Center, 301 Court Ave., Park Rapids, MN 56470, phone 218-732-3552. Property Records covers valuation and classification, homestead, tax reduction programs and recording of real estate documents, so a single visit can cover a value question and a deed.

When are Hubbard County property taxes due and what are the penalties?

Minnesota Statutes 279.01 sets two halves, payable before May 16 and before October 16 when a parcel's tax is over $100. A parcel at or under $100 is due in full with the first half. A payment mailed and postmarked by the due date is on time, and the treasurer must abate the penalty once if the postmark falls within one business day after.

Late payment penalties under Minnesota Statutes 279.01
StageHomesteadNonhomestead
Day after the due date2%4%
First day of the next monthAnother 2%Another 4%
